input:
A 63-year-old woman presented to our department with a 6-month history of recurrent vomiting and loss of 5 kg in weight. The patient had a medical history of dyslipidaemia and hypertension; she was prescribed rosuvastatin and olmesartan. She had no history of gastrointestinal disorders, recent foreign travel, or infection with Helicobacter pylori.
On examination, she was generally unwell and underweight; her blood pressure was 150/88 mm Hg, pulse was 70 beats per min, oxygen saturation was 99%, and BMI was 16 kg/m2. We found no lymphadenopathy, and abdominal examination found no masses or ascites.
Laboratory investigations showed normal complete blood count—including a typical eosinophil count; carcinoembryonic antigen, soluble interleukin-2 receptor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody tests were within normal range. Antinuclear antibody titre was 1:160 (normal value <1:40) and serum immunoglobulin E was 700 IU/mL (typical range 0–100).
An oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) showed a distended stomach with linear scars and a rough atrophic mucosa that bled easily upon contact (figure). Histopathological examination of a sample obtained by gastric biopsy showed subepithelial collagen deposition with inflammatory cell infiltration—including eosinophils (figure); the small and large intestines showed no specific findings.
At this stage, our working diagnosis included collagenous gastritis, eosinophilic gastritis, and autoimmune gastritis. And based on these working diagnoses, the patient was prescribed a proton pump inhibitor—esomeprazole 20 mg orally—which did not result in any improvement.
Further review of the medical history found that the patient had been taking olmesartan 20 mg daily for the past decade and we considered that it may have been responsible for the patient's symptoms; we therefore decided to stop it.
2 weeks later, the patient stopped vomiting and within 2 months she had gained 7 kg. A repeat OGD, 6 months post-discontinuation, showed a substantial improvement in mucosal inflammation; histopathological examination of samples obtained by biopsies, showed no evidence of residual collagen bands or significant inflammatory cell infiltration (appendix). And at 2 years after discontinuation of the olmesartan no recurrence was seen. Regarding the patient's hypertension, azelnidipine 8 mg daily was prescribed as an alternative treatment.
Collagenous gastritis is characterised by patchy subepithelial collagen bands and inflammatory cell infiltration, including eosinophils; such features can appear in other types of gastritis with similar inflammatory cell infiltration—including eosinophilic gastritis, coeliac disease, and autoimmune gastritis—necessitating a high index of suspicion to make an accurate pathological diagnosis. The precise pathogenesis of collagenous gastritis remains poorly understood and no available treatments are established owing to its rarity; associations with certain medications—including olmesartan as in our patient—have been suggested.

options: Administration of steroids, Discontinuation of olmesartan, Gluten-free diet, Administration of proton pump inhibitors

input: A 41-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of progressive vision loss and headaches. MRI revealed a large sellar tumour with suprasellar extension, which was deemed a probable pituitary macroadenoma (figure A, B). The patient underwent transsphenoidal surgery because of visual field defects and headaches. Histological analysis after surgery revealed a giant cell tumour of bone (GCTB) and symptoms improved; however, 2 months later the large sellar–clival remnant compressing the optic chiasm (figure C, D) motivated a second surgery by pterional craniotomy. After surgery, tumour regrowth occurred (figure E, F), causing diplopia and blurred vision. A third decompressing operation aiming for maximal debulking before denosumab commencement was done endoscopically; however, only partial tumour removal was achieved (figure G, H). Denosumab (120 mg subcutaneously every 28 days) was initiated, and a marked response was noted after 6 months of treatment (figure I, J). After 14 months of denosumab, the patient remained symptom-free without needing further operations (figure K, L).GCTB represent 5–10% of bone tumours, classically affect long bones (<1% of all GCTB have a cranial location) and, although benign, can be locally aggressive. GCTB are histologically characterised by large multinucleated giant cells, but the clinical or radiological differential diagnosis can be challenging. Denosumab, an inhibitor of receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL), can be used to treat GCTB, because RANKL is overexpressed by mononuclear neoplastic stromal cells. As shown here, denosumab should also be considered in the early management of sellar–clival GCTB. This case also highlights the sustained reduction in tumour mass achieved by denosumab, sparing the patient from further operations. If feasible, surgical resection is still preferable as the definitive treatment, because the effect of denosumab wears off after stopping treatment and tumour regrowth can occur. Lifelong denosumab treatment will thus be likely required in this case; however, increasing the intervals between denosumab administration can be attempted to prevent or minimise adverse events, such as osteonecrosis of the jaw or atypical femoral fractures. Although GCTB is usually managed by rheumatologists, oncologists, or orthopaedics, sellar or parasellar GCTB might be first seen by endocrinologists, ophthalmologists, or neurosurgeons, who should be aware of this entity and the potential role of denosumab in its management.
options: Meningioma, Pituitary tumour, Giant cell tumour of bone, Germinoma

A 35-year-old woman complaining of weakness of her left arm and leg was admitted to our hospital. She said the problem started 25 h earlier, soon after liposuction on her left thigh and a filler injection of the fat into her face in a beauty salon. The woman was previously healthy with no medical history. On physical examination we found hemiplegia of the left limbs: muscle strength was 1/5 in the arm and 3/5 in the leg. She had left central facial palsy and clear speech, and was cognitively intact. Bilateral Babinski signs were negative and there were no features of meningeal irritation. The patient's blood pressure, pulse rate, and temperature were in the normal ranges. Routine blood tests, blood lipids, glucose concentration, and electrolytes were also normal. An electrocardiogram and a transthoracic echocardiogram showed no abnormalities.A CT scan of the woman's brain showed a low-density strip (appendix) in the right middle cerebral artery (MCA) that was hyperintense on T1, T2, and T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery weighted MRIs (figure; appendix). Additionally, the MRI showed an area of infarction in the region supplied by the right MCA. Magnetic resonance angiography (appendix) showed an occlusion of part of the right MCA and a low-density filling defect in the initial segment of the right external carotid artery—which, on an ultrasound scan, was hyperechoic—indicative of an embolus (figure).
Considering all the information in the round, we decided that the patient had a cerebral fat embolism (CFE) following the injection into her face of autologous fat. We decided to treat her conservatively with oral aspirin 0·2 g once daily, oral atorvastatin 40 mg once daily, and intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg once daily. After 1 week, the patient's symptoms began to resolve and after 2 weeks she was transferred to the rehabilitation department. 3 months after she came into hospital, she was able to walk unaided.
A stroke in a young person can be caused by emboli, atherosclerotic disease, vasculopathies, or subarachnoid or intraparenchymal bleeding. Other causes particularly important in the younger age group are oral contraceptive use, pregnancy and postpartum states, substance use, trauma, and migraine. CFE—a thankfully rarely reported complication of cosmetic procedures—more usually occurs after fractures of the long bones.
How the fat from an autologous facial filler reaches the arterial network is unclear. It may be that during the injection the needle penetrates a small artery. Then, possibly due to continuous pressure applied during the injection, the fat travels, against the normal blood flow, up the small artery, through the facial artery and the external carotid artery, into the internal carotid artery.
CFE is usually self-limiting. The key with a presentation of rapid onset of left-sided weakness—such as in our patient—is to make the right diagnosis as soon as possible.

options: Respiratory distress, Rash, Long-bone fracture in the legs, Altered mental state

A 20-year-old woman presented with a history of right-sided headaches associated with rapid worsening of vision in the right eye over a period of a few days. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity of finger counting close to the face and a relative afferent pupillary defect was found in the right eye. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed retinal vasculitis with extensive perivascular sheathing resembling a so-called frosted branch appearance with disc oedema and haemorrhages (figure A, video). There were haemorrhages in the posterior pole with vascular sheathing (vasculitis) along the inferiotemporal vascular arcade (figure B). Fundus fluorescence angiography of the right eye revealed disc leakage with perivascular leakage and blocked fluorescence at the macula (figure C). Optical coherence tomography revealed macular oedema. The left eye was healthy. Blood tests revealed anaemia, lymphopenia with an absolute CD4 count of 149 cells per mm3 (normal range: 500–1500 cells per mm3), reduced glomerular filtration rate, blood urea concentration of 131 mg/dL, serum creatinine concentration of 4·9 mg/dL, and microscopic haematuria with occasional red blood cell casts. 24-h urinary protein concentration was 2·8 g. Blood serology for viruses, including HIV, was negative. Vitreous fluid testing for cytomegalovirus DNA was negative. Blood autoantibody panel showed myeloperoxidase antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) ELISA positivity with 101 U/mL (normal range: <5 U/mL). A kidney biopsy was completed for histopathological investigation and hematoxylin and eosin staining used, which revealed necrotising crescentic nephritis (figure D) and many fibrotic crescents along with interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy, no different test or stain was used, these pathological features were not visible in the image. Immunofluorescence revealed an absence of immune complexes (figure E). A diagnosis of microscopic polyangiitis with frosted branch angiitis of the retina and pauci-immune necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis was made. The patient was treated with corticosteroids (three intravenous pulses of methylprednisone followed by oral prednisone with a starting dose of 1 mg/kg per day) and oral cyclophosphamide (2 mg/kg per day in 2 divided doses), which resulted in a gradual improvement of vision in the affected right eye. After 3 months of treatment, at the last outpatient visit, her creatinine concentration had decreased to 2·4 mg/dL, she had a blood urea concentration of 65 mg/dL, and her haemoglobin and CD4 counts improved. At 3 months post-disgnosis proteinuria had decreased to 1·1 g/24 h. Visual acuity in the right eye had improved to 6/36. Fundus examination showed marked resolution of retinal vasculitis with a few haemorrhages.
The term frosted branch angiitis encompasses a rare, vision-threatening, non-occlusive retinal perivasculitis with perivascular exudate causing severe retinal vessel sheathing resembling frosted tree branches. Retinal frosted branch angiitis is classified into three categories: type 1, associated with malignancy (leukaemia or lymphoma); type 2, associated with viral or bacterial infections, or autoimmune conditions; and type 3, primary idiopathic. Rheumatological disorders associated with retinal frosted branch angiitis include granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome, sarcoidosis, and Behçet's disease. In ANCA-associated vasculitis, lymphopenia with a low disease-related CD4 count is not uncommon, and is due to increased activation of CD4 T cells and their redistribution to the vessels and tissues. A low CD4 count has also been shown to be a risk factor for developing retinal vasculitis. Retinal vasculitis in ANCA-associated vasculitis is a rare occurrence and is an occlusive vasculopathy resulting from fibrinoid necrosis and secondary thrombosis. However, a few cases of frosted branch angiitis have been reported with granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis. The hypothesis for frosted branch angiitis in ANCA-associated vasculitis is that it represents an extreme form of a diffuse perivasculitis with movement of inflammatory cells in large numbers from the vascular wall into the retina causing sheathing due to inflammation-induced disruption of the blood retinal barrier. In this patient, the relative compartmentalisation of CD4 lymphocytes in the retinal vasculature could have caused the peripheral lymphopenia.
The outcome of primary idiopathic frosted branch angiitis is favourable with a good response to corticosteroids. The outcome of secondary frosted branch angiitis (ie, type 1 and 2), including that in ANCA-associated vasculitis, is variable and is negatively influenced by the severity of the underlying disorder and the delay in diagnosis.

output: Secondary frosted branch angiitis has been reported in association with granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis

A 76-year-old man who had a 2-day history being unwell—starting with sweating and a fever that then developed into delirium—was admitted to the emergency room of a local general hospital; he then had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure without recovering consciousness. The patient was transferred to our intensive care unit after orotracheal intubation and initiation of invasive mechanical ventilation.
1 month earlier, the patient had radiofrequency catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation refractory to both medication and electrical cardioversion. The patient had a medical history of atrial fibrillation, hypertension, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease; he was prescribed apixaban, bisoprolol, dapagliflozin, furosemide, and metformin.
On examination, the patient was in a coma—Glasgow Coma Score 6; pupils were reactive and symmetrical. He had no sensory or motor deficits or focal neurological signs. Blood pressure was 113/52 mm Hg, heart rate 83 beats per min, oxygen saturation was in typical range, and temperature was 39·6°C.
Laboratory investigations found a biological inflammatory syndrome (C-reactive protein concentration was 177 mg/L [typical range <10]; white blood cell count was 15 000 per mm [typical range 4000–10 000]; and troponin was 3309 ng/L [typical range <5]).
A CT scan of the patient's brain showed diffuse pneumocephalus (figure); brain ischaemia was confirmed by hyperintense signals on MRI FLAIR T2-weighted sequences (figure).
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy was immediately started which effectively dissolved the cerebral air embolism (appendix); the patient had two sessions, 24 h apart, in our hyperbaric chamber receiving invasive mechanical ventilation—3 atmospheres of pressure with the fraction of inspired oxygen at 100% for 2 h.
We suspected the cerebral air embolism had come from an atrio-oesophageal fistula by a process of elimination: none of the common sources of pneumocephalus—including an intravenous line, or a recent endoscopy or laparoscopy—were identified in our patient. The absence of any abnormalities on clinical examination and the recent history of catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation further added to our conviction of an atrio-oesophageal fistula.
A chest CT angiogram showed a filiform hypodense signal within the left atrium anterior to the opening of the right inferior pulmonary vein and extending to the posterior wall of the left atrium communicating with the oesophagus, suggestive of an atrio-oesophageal fistula (figure). Delayed phase contrast-enhanced CT scanning showed recurrence of an air bubble in the left atrium—confirming air leakage (figure).
The patient had surgery to close the fistula with oesophagostomy immediately on completion of the hyperbaric oxygen therapy and more than 24 h after the onset of symptoms. However, due to the presence of diffuse brain ischaemia seen on MRI done prior to the hyperbaric oxygen therapy and following discussion with the patient's relatives, active treatment was withdrawn. The patient died 1 week after admission to the intensive care unit.
Atrio-oesophageal fistula complicating catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation can—as in our patient—result in air embolism. Cerebral air embolism can result in acute ischaemia and cerebral oedema that may mimic the presentation of other stroke syndromes; prompt hyperbaric oxygen therapy is the mainstay of treatment.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy decreases the size of bubbles because of an increase in ambient pressure and a rapid lowering of nitrogen levels that optimises oxygenation of poorly perfused brain tissue; it remains the gold standard treatment for cerebral air embolism with excellent results when initiated immediately.
image_path: ./data/images/lancet_images/Cerebral air embolism and hyperbaric oxygen therapy.jpg
output: Atrio-oesophageal fistula complicating atrial fibrillation radiofrequency ablation
target: Atrio-oesophageal fistula complicating atrial fibrillation radiofrequency ablation
options: Alveolar rupture due to invasive mechanical ventilation, Crohn's disease incidentally discovered, Suicide attempt with intravascular air injection, Atrio-oesophageal fistula complicating atrial fibrillation radiofrequency ablation

input: A 61-year-old who was receiving long-term treatment with prednisone for refractory idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura required a dose increase after a large decrease in platelet count (6×109/L). He had had his spleen removed 7 years earlier. He was not on any other medication and there was no evidence of pseudothrombocytopenia, lymphoprolipherative disease, malignancies, or Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Serological tests were negative for HIV, Epstein Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, antinuclear antibodies, and lupus anticoagulant. Stool specimen was negative for Helicobacter pylori. 24 h later he developed pigmented vesicles on the left side of his trunk, left arm, and left hand. Segmental distribution of the painful cutaneous lesions suggested haemorrhagic herpes zoster. Prednisone was stopped and the patient was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin G (1 g/kg daily for 4 days) and valacyclovir (1 g three times daily). He had a rapid increase in platelet count and uneventful recovery. Haemorrhagic herpes zoster is an atypical form of cutaneous varicella zoster virus and correlates with immunodepression, coagulopathy, or thrombocytopenia.
options: Melanoma, Aedes aegypi bites, Herpes zoster infection, Kaposis sarcoma

input: A 60-year-old Japanese man was referred to our hospital because of an abnormal endoscopic finding in the oesophagus at a regular health check. He reported receiving no medication and had no history of alcohol misuse. The patient was a former smoker and reported sometimes feeling heartburn. Laboratory data revealed no pronounced abnormalities. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed short segment Barrett's oesophagus and a whitish elevated lesion adjacent to the Barrett's oesophagus lesion (figure, A). Vessel structures could not be seen by magnified narrow band imaging, because of a whitish plaque (figure, B). Chromoendoscopy with Lugol's iodine solution showed decreased staining of the lesion (figure, C). A biopsy was done, and histology confirmed cell proliferation of the squamous epithelium. Although cellular atypicality was mild, we considered the lesion to be potentially malignant. Therefore, an endoscopic submucosal dissection was done for an en-bloc complete resection and diagnosis. Histology showed papillary growth and nests of well differentiated squamous epithelium pushing into the underlying stroma, which is typical of oesophageal verrucous carcinoma (figure, D). Pathological examination revealed tumour depth invasion into the lamina propria mucosa (stage T1a) without lymphovascular invasion. The patient was monitored closely and no recurrence had occurred at 3 months after the endoscopic submucosal dissection.Oesophageal verrucous carcinoma is a very rare malignancy. Although, the cause of such lesions is debated, it has been suggested that oesophageal verrucous carcinoma is associated with achalasia, acid reflux, and alcohol and nicotine misuse. The common endoscopic appearance of most oesophageal verrucous carcinomas is an elevated whitish plaque that is clearly circumscribed. Oesophageal verrucous carcinomas are difficult to diagnose before surgical resection. Accurate diagnosis is often delayed because the endoscopic finding of a whitish plaque is similar to a Candida infection and squamous cell papilloma. In addition, superficial biopsies are frequently false negative for malignancy because of highly differentiated histology. Endoscopic resection can be curative for oesophageal verrucous carcinoma restricted to the epithelium and the lamina propria mucosa. A lack of recognition of oesophageal verrucous carcinoma leads to a delay in diagnosis and progression of the disease. To improve the chance of curative treatment, endoscopists need to recognise the macroscopic findings and frequent difficulties associated with diagnosis of oesophageal verrucous carcinoma.
options: Adenocarcinoma, Squamous cell papilloma, Candida oesophagitis, Verrucous carcinoma

On Oct 16, 2015, a 55-year-old woman presented to the liver clinic with jaundice, months of progressive abdominal discomfort, and enlarged superficial veins on her abdomen. She had a history of hepatic sarcoidosis, diagnosed 6 years previously. Clinical examination revealed jaundice, massive hepatomegaly, moderate splenomegaly, and dilated superficial veins, both above and below the umbilicus.Further investigation with abdominal ultrasound and CT scans of the liver revealed Budd-Chiari syndrome, in addition to inferior vena cava thrombus. Inferior vena cava occlusion results in collaterisation along the abdominal wall from the inferior epigastric and superficial epigastric veins below the umbilicus, which drain into a recanalised paraumbilical vein. Our patient had large and dilated superficial abdominal veins both above and below the umbilicus (figure, A).
A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) was inserted proximal to the thrombus from the hepatic portion of the inferior vena cava into the main portal vein, and the patient was started on anticoagulation with warfarin. Repeated CT scanning revealed a patent TIPS, prominent abdominal wall veins (figure, B), and an occluded hepatic vein and inferior vena cava (figure, C). The patient had extensive thrombophilia testing, including testing for JAK2 mutation, lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin antibodies, anti-β2 glycoprotein antibodies, protein C and S concentrations, paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, and factor V Leiden. All test results were normal, and both the Budd-Chiari syndrome and inferior vena cava occlusion were attributed to thrombophilia associated with hepatic sarcoidosis. TIPS was successful at reducing the patient's portal hypertension, as evidenced by improved bilirubin (from 155 μmol/L before to 24 μmol/L after the procedure) and reduced size of peri-portal collateral vessels on subsequent imaging. The patient later developed multiple TIPS occlusions, one of which occurred in the context of a subtherapeutic international normalised ratio, associated with worsening complications of cirrhosis. The patient has now successfully undergone orthotopic liver transplantation.
options: Caput medusae from cirrhosis and portal hypertension, Superior vena cava obstruction, Pelvic congestion syndrome, Inferior vena cava obstruction

input: A 26-year-old man was referred to our orthopaedics department with left thigh pain. Radiography and CT revealed a cortical mass unilaterally on the medial side of the distal femoral diaphysis (figure A, B). The lesion extended with osteoblastic and osteolytic changes that accompany a periosteal reaction. MRI revealed a contrast-enhanced soft tissue mass surrounding the cortical lesion (figure C–E). No major blood vessel or bone marrow infiltration was observed. Our primary differential diagnosis was malignancy, particularly periosteal osteosarcoma, followed by fracture, osteomyelitis, or periostitis. A periosteal biopsy did not show malignancy but did reveal neutrophilic inflammation (figure F, G). Additional testing showed elevated inflammatory markers and arterial wall thickening in the aortic arch and its common branches (figure H) but not in the left femoral artery. At follow-up 2 months after the first visit, the patient reported general fatigue. Carotid bruits and blood pressure differences between the arms were observed. The patient was diagnosed with Takayasu arteritis based on the American College of Rheumatology–European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology classification criteria. Treatment of Takayasu arteritis was initiated using daily oral prednisolone (initial dose of 80 mg followed by decreasing dose thereafter) followed by subcutaneous tocilizumab (162 mg/week), after which the left thigh pain disappeared and periostitis subsided on imaging (figure I–K). The patient's Indian Takayasu Clinical Activity Score decreased from 6 to 2. We concluded that the femoral lesions were associated with Takayasu arteritis. Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis that presents with non-specific symptoms and signs, but periostitis is a rare manifestation. Isolated bone lesions incline the diagnosis more towards malignancy than systemic disease; however, several previous reports have shown isolated Takayasu arteritis-associated periostitis. Local inflammation of the periosteum might create a malignancy-like mass and periosteal osteosarcoma is suspected when the mass affects the femoral diaphysis in young adults. As patient presentation and imaging findings of Takayasu arteritis-associated periostitis might mimic periosteal osteosarcoma, it is imperative to rule out malignancy and maintain a broad differential diagnosis.

options: Osteomyelitis, Osteoblastoma, Periosteal osteosarcoma, Takayasu arteritis-associated periostitis

A 41-year-old man presented to our rheumatology clinic with a 2-month history of symmetric inflammatory polyarthralgia and pleuritic chest pain. 1 year before, he had visited another hospital reporting a dry cough; 2 months later he returned to the same institution complaining of breathlessness and fatigue; at that time, pulmonary tuberculosis and heart failure had been ruled out.Notably, in his occupational history, 11 years before his current health difficulties, he had finished 6 years of employment in a factory producing glass and fibreglass, in Medellin, Colombia. The patient's main tasks had been in the blending process: mixing sand and soda ash, cutting, polishing, and repairing flat glass and fibreglass. He worked 9-h days in a poorly ventilated workspace and used personal protection equipment for less than 30 min per h. The patient had smoked one to two cigarettes daily for the past 26 years and stopped 4 months before his current presentation.
On examination he was well looking and not distressed; he had bilateral effusions in his wrist, metacarpophalangeal, and knee joints. Crackles were audible at the apex of his right lung.
Laboratory investigations showed positive antinuclear antibodies—at a titre of 1:320, homogeneous pattern—and raised anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies (ACPAs; 37 UI/ml; reference value <5). Rheumatoid factor was negative.
A digital chest x-ray showed scattered and tiny lung nodules, cavitation in the right upper lobe, and consolidation at the left upper lobe (figure). A CT scan showed cavitation and numerous nodules between 1 mm and 5 mm in size, with some confluent areas, randomly distributed throughout the lungs (figure).
Ziehl-Neelsen staining, nucleic acid amplification test, and culture for Mycobacterium tuberculosis of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid were negative. Histopathological analysis of a sample obtained by thoracoscopically guided open lung biopsy showed multiple granulomas with a central necrotic area, surrounded by layers of crystal silica and mononuclear infiltrate, without neoplasm or acid-fast bacteria (appendix). Considering the patient's occupational history, signs, and symptoms, and findings on investigation, we diagnosed accelerated silicosis complicated by Caplan syndrome—mimicking a miliary pattern and cavitary disease. At 6 months’ follow-up, spirometry testing showed FEV1/FVC (%) 95% (0,77), FVC 145·0% (7,14 L), and FEV1 138% (5,5 L).
At 12 months’ follow-up, the patient continued to report a dry cough and dyspnoea on exertion; original x-ray findings remained unchanged. However, treatment with rituximab, methotrexate, and prednisolone had improved the condition of the patient's painful, swollen knee and hand joints.
Caplan syndrome is a rare complication of silicosis—incidence between 0·75% and 0·89%—characterised by pulmonary nodules and rheumatoid arthritis in patients with pneumoconiosis.
The relationship between silicosis and rheumatoid arthritis development has been the subject of much debate. Disease development begins when respirable crystalline silica dust is engulfed by macrophages producing lysosomal dysfunction. Cell death results in exposure of sequestered antigens, NALP3 inflammasome activation, production of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, IL-1β and TNF-α), and activation of T and B cells (eg, T-reg with production of IL-10 and TGF-β which produces fibrosis, and T-helper CD4+ cell responses). These changes lead to the formation of autoantibodies and immune complexes—including rheumatoid factor and ACPAs—which ultimately lead to synovial cell activation, infiltration, inflammation, neoangiogenesis, and joint tissue destruction.
Tuberculosis and lung cancer—at high risk in patients with silicosis—need to be excluded before diagnosing Caplan syndrome since all three can produce cavity lung lesions and miliary pattern on imaging.
options: Tuberculosis, Sarcoidosis, Lymphangitic carcinomatosis, Caplan syndrome

A 17-year-old boy was referred to the ophthalmology service at St Thomas' Hospital (London, UK) with bilateral red eyes, bilateral eye pain independent of eye movement that disturbed his sleep, photophobia, and mild, subjective blurring of vision. He had become infected with SARS-CoV-2 5 weeks before referral and had been diagnosed with paediatric inflammatory multisystem syndrome temporally associated with COVID-19 (PIMS-TS) and associated myocarditis.His Snellen visual acuity was excellent: 6/4 unaided in both eyes. He had bilateral, diffuse episcleral and deep scleral injection (vasodilatation with hyperaemia) that did not blanch with topical 10% phenylephrine; a bilateral anterior chamber grading of 2+ (16–25 cells in a 1 mm × 1 mm field); no vitritis, retinitis, or vasculitis; and an otherwise unremarkable fundal examination (figure A, B). A B-scan ultrasound did not show any posterior scleritis. He was diagnosed with bilateral, diffuse, anterior non-necrotising scleritis with anterior uveitis.
Before his ophthalmology referral, the patient had been treated for PIMS-TS with a 3-day course of intravenous methylprednisolone (950 mg/day). He subsequently developed fever, had a rising C-reactive protein concentration 1 week post-admission (from 47 mg/L to 94 mg/L over the course of 1 day), and received 800 mg of intravenous tocilizumab on the day of his referral. After attending the ophthalmology service, he started a course of oral prednisolone (starting dose 40 mg/day for 17 days), guttae 0·1% dexamethasone (eye drops to both eyes at an initial schedule of once every 2 h for 3 days), and a 1-week course of guttae 1% cyclopentolate (eye drops to both eyes twice daily). Treatment (prednisolone and guttae 0·1% dexamethasone) was tapered over a 6-week period. 7 days after ophthalmology referral and review, the patient's symptoms had resolved and he had normal vision and no ongoing inflammation.
10 days after referral, the patient presented with a right facial (VIIth) nerve palsy and his prescribed regimen of prednisolone (40 mg/day, before tapering) was not changed. Neuroimaging showed mild inflammation of the right tympanic facial nerve (figure 1C). Prompt resolution of facial weakness occurred within 4 weeks.
It is imperative not to misdiagnose the potentially sight-threatening conditions of scleritis and uveitis as conjunctivitis, which is the commonly known ophthalmic association in PIMS-TS.
options: Viral conjunctivitis, Acute glaucoma, Episcleritis, Anterior uveitis and scleritis

input:
A 61-year-old woman with a 4-day history of asthenia, fever, and a rash was seen by our team in the hospital intensive care unit.
The patient had clear cell renal cell carcinoma with tumoral thrombosis of the right renal vein and inferior vena cava. She was being treated with a checkpoint inhibitor, pembrolizumab—a PD-1 inhibitor—and the endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGF-R) tyrosine kinase inhibitor, axitinib, before re-assessment for surgery, in the oncology day hospital unit. 3 days after the third infusion of pembrolizumab, the patient had been admitted to the intensive care unit because she had become haemodynamically unstable; she had developed heart failure, and purpura fulminans (figure; appendix) over her arms and legs, which had initially appeared as livedo racemose a few hours before. She had also been found to have an ascending sensory motor deficit of her lower limbs.
On examination, we found the patient to be unwell; her blood pressure was 90/60 mm Hg, pulse 30 beats per min, oxygen saturation was 100% on 15 L/min oxygen, and temperature was 32°C. She was confused, with a Glasgow Coma Score of 8 (eye opening response 2, verbal response 2, and motor response 4). She needed both noradrenaline and dobutamine because of her cardiac failure. Additionally, the patient was being treated with meropenem and amikacin; axitinib had been stopped at the point of admission to the intensive care unit.
Laboratory investigations showed high concentrations of N-terminal-pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (10 518 pg/mL; typical level <125 in people younger than 75 years) and troponin (109 ng/L; typical level <14). Concentrations of liver enzymes and thyroid-stimulating hormone were elevated; C-reactive protein concentration was 36 mg/L (typical range 8–10). Analysis of a sample of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed an elevated protein concentration (0·52 g/L; typical level <0·4) and a normal white blood cell count; cultures of blood, CSF, urine, and skin showed no abnormalities.
PCR skin swab testing was negative for Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae, resulting in the cessation of antibiotics treatment.
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed diffuse thickening of the wall of the colon; echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 25% (normal range 50–70). MRIs of brain and spinal cord showed no abnormalities. An electromyogram showed severe sensory-motor neurogenic damage compatible with axonal length-dependent processes without demyelination.
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a skin biopsy showed thrombosis with leukocytoclastic vasculitis, which, considering the patient's presentation, investigations, and history in the round, led us to conclude she had developed an immune-induced myocarditis, acute motor and sensory axonal polyneuropathy, colitis, hypothyroidism, hepatitis, and purpura fulminans.
The patient was commenced on pulse methylprednisolone (1 g per day for 5 days) and intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g per kg over 4 days), which resulted in the improvement of her general condition. She had three separate plasma exchanges to clear the pembrolizumab and surgery of the deepest wounds with skin grafts.
The corticosteroids were gradually tapered down over the next 4 months, and at follow-up 6 months later the skin lesions had completely healed. The patient's neoplastic disease was under control—despite discontinuation of the pembrolizumab and axitinib.
Immune checkpoint inhibitors have become established treatments for several cancers including malignant melanoma and renal cell carcinoma. Such developments have, in some patients resulted, in treatment-related adverse effects of variable severity. Immune-related purpura fulminans associated with pembrolizumab has been reported previously in a patient treated for lung carcinoma.

An 80-year-old man with a 12-h history of watery diarrhoea was admitted to our hospital. Notably, the patient had 2 similar episodes in the previous month; on each occasion his condition had improved after a short stay on the ward treated with fluid resuscitation using balanced crystalloids and oxygen. He had a history of hypertension and was prescribed olmesartan. He reported no recent foreign travel.
On examination, the patient was unwell with signs of hypovolemic shock; his blood pressure was 72/51 mm Hg, pulse 128 beats per min, respiratory rate 33 breaths per min, and temperature was 36·2°C. His urine output was 7 mL per h (normal range 25–30).
Laboratory investigations indicated that the patient was in acute renal failure; he was negative for tests for infectious diseases—including HIV, norovirus, rotavirus, Clostridium difficile, Campylobacter spp, invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella, Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi, Salmonella enterica serotype Paratyphi, and Shigella spp. Autoimmune testing for antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, anti-smooth muscle antibody, antimitochondrial antibodies and anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies, antiendomysial antibodies, antiparietal cell antibodies, and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies was negative.
Point-of-care ultrasonography using a convex probe for abdominal imaging showed no ascites or bowel wall thickening. The patient was resuscitated using isotonic crystalloid fluid; we then did an upper endoscopy and colonoscopy which also showed no significant macroscopic abnormalities.
Histopathological examination of a sample of a duodenal biopsy showed severe villous blunting with crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial T cells; subepithelial foci of sprue-type collagenous thickening were identified (figure).Considering the case in the round, we made a diagnosis of olmesartan-associated sprue-like enteropathy; using the Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale—often referred to as the Naranjo Scale—the patient obtained a score of 9, indicating a definite drug reaction. The olmesartan was discontinued and the patient's diarrhoea improved; he had no further admissions. At 6 months follow-up, he reported no diarrhoea; an upper endoscopy showed that the mucosal atrophy had mostly healed.
Olmesartan—a widely used antihypertensive which acts by blocking the angiotensin II receptor—is a rare cause of severe enteropathy that should be considered as differential diagnosis in cases of severe diarrhoea and weight loss. Pathological mechanisms underlying the enteropathy are unknown. Mean duration of olmesartan therapy before patients developed symptoms is very variable: from 6 months to 7 years. The long delay suggests cell-mediated immunity damage is involved. Histological findings at duodenal biopsy can mimic celiac disease or collagenous sprue, so clinicopathological correlation is essential to confirm the diagnosis. Other diseases to be considered in the differential diagnosis include tropical sprue, autoimmune enteropathy, inflammatory bowel disease—Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis—and, of course, reactions to other medications. Regarding treatment, immediate discontinuation of the Olmesartan will quickly resolve the problem.
target: The diarrhoea usually begins within the first 24 hr of starting olmesartan
options: Celiac disease is an important differential diagnosis, The diarrhoea usually begins within the first 24 hr of starting olmesartan, Treatment involves stopping olmesartan, Histopathological features include severe villous blunting

A 47-year-old woman with well controlled HIV (CD4 >1000 cells per μL and an undetectable viral load) presented to our hospital with confusion and seizures. Results of brain MRI were unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed lymphocytosis (20 cells per μL), a high protein concentration (0·52 g/L), and a low glucose concentration (3·2 mmol/L in CSF vs 8·1 mmol/L in serum). CT chest images revealed a cavitating lesion in the left upper lobe of the lung, with surrounding tree-in-bud opacities. Tuberculosis treatment (rifabutin 150 mg per day, pyrazinamide 2 g per day, moxifloxacin 400 mg per day, isoniazid 300 mg per day) and dexamethasone (4 mg four times a day) were started, and she was followed up as an outpatient. Fully sensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis subsequently grew from a bronchoalveolar lavage.1 month later, she presented to the emergency department with a 2 day history of fever, haemoptysis, and drowsiness. She had a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 10 (eye opening 4 points; verbal response 1 point; motor response 5 points), extension of the left big toe during the plantar response test, and a right gaze preference. Chest CT showed that the lesion in the left upper lobe of the lung had shrunk, but new lesions had appeared in the right upper lobe and left lower lobe. Multiple brain lesions were present on MRI (figure). Biopsy of the lesion in the right upper lobe of the lung revealed multiple fungal hyphae consistent with aspergillus. Liposomal amphotericin B (450 mg daily) was started. Aspergillus fumigatus subsequently grew from the biopsy sample and from a bronchoaleveolar lavage.
Her GCS score dropped to 8 the day after admission and she was intubated and ventilated. Serial CTs showed new areas of haemorrhage within the pre-existing brain lesions. 8 days after admission, her pupils became fixed and dilated, and brain CT showed herniation of the cerebellar tonsils into foramen magnum. She died 1 day later. Collateral history from a relative revealed that the patient had a history of heavy cannabis use.
Invasive aspergillosis has been reported a handful of times in association with cannabis use, usually in patients with advanced immunosuppression. Dexamethasone probably led to an immunosuppressive state in the patient despite well controlled HIV infection, in the context of repeated aspergillus exposure through regular use of aspergillus-contaminated cannabis.

options: Tuberculosis, Toxoplasmosis, Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, Disseminated aspergillosis

input: A 57-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of shortness of breath and dizziness. The physical examination was notable for pallor. The results of hemoglobin electrophoresis and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase testing were normal, and methemoglobin and direct antiglobulin tests were negative. A peripheral blood smear (left, Giemsa staining) showed poikilocytosis, nucleated red cells (black arrows), and polychromatic cells (white arrows). The peripheral blood smear also showed bite cells (left, red arrows), blister cells (left, asterisks), and erythrocyte inclusions (middle, Giemsa staining). input: A 56-year-old woman presented with a 1 year history of horns growing on the proximal interphalangeal joints of the right index and middle fingers. 3 years previously, the patient had undergone traumatic amputation of these fingers. The patient was not in an immunocompromised state. Physical examination showed opaque, yellowish, scabrous horny outgrowths on the amputated stumps of the proximal interphalangeal joints (figure A). The hyperkeratotic horns showed fungal hyphae on microscopy and grew Trichophyton rubrum in microbiological cultures. A diagnosis of ringworm of the finger was made. The lesions improved after treatment with oral itraconazole at 400 mg per day for 1 week and topical salicylic acid, without relapse (figure B).Ringworm species invade the stratum corneum of the skin, and damage keratinised tissues. T rubrum often induces the clinical feature of hyperkeratosis in tinea pedis. It is the main cause of onychomycosis and leads to thickened nail plates. Moreover, T rubrum can form cutaneous horns, as occurred in the present case.

input: A 64-year-old male farmer presented to our hospital in April, 2013, with a 3 month history of painless, progressive swelling of his chest wall and lower jaw, and 10 kg unintentional weight loss. On examination he had multiple lumps about 3 × 1·5 cm around the angle of the mandible, and multiple 10 × 8 cm lumps at the mid sternal region and of the left lower anterior chest wall (figure). These lumps were non-tender to palpation, hard, and tethered, with irregular contours, no tempertature changes or overlying skin changes. Blood tests were normal and HIV serology was negative. CT Chest showed a soft tissue mass 8 × 10·6 × 8 cm encasing and eroding the body of sternum with presternal and retrosternal soft tissue components (appendix), and whole-body PET CT fusion showed increased 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) uptake (appendix). Histological and immunohistochemical examination of a biopsy specimen from the chest wall swelling showed tightly-packed small round cells with high mitotic activity infiltrating fat and starry sky appearance (figure), positive for CD20, Bcl-2, Mum-1, and Bcl-6, and negative for CD10, CD3, Cyclin-D1, and TdT, with Ki-67 nearly 100%. Conventional cytogenetics showed complex structural and numerical abnormalities including characteristic t (8;14) (appendix). We diagnosed high risk group adult Burkitt lymphoma stage IV, and started treatment with modified Magrath regimen of four alternating cycles of R-CODOX-M and R-IMVAC chemotherapy. The patient achieved complete remission with disappearance of sternal swellings, normal peripheral blood counts, normal bone marrow aspirate, and no evidence of 18FDG uptake on repeat PET scan. He remained in remission at last 3 month follow-up in December, 2013.
options: Burkitt’s lymphoma, Follicular lymphoma, Multiple plasmocytoma, Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

input:
A 17-year-old German student with acute abdominal pain attended a regional hospital in northern Germany. During interview, he said that 2 weeks earlier his ejaculate had changed to a yellowish brown colour. Laboratory analysis showed leucocytosis (21·9 × 109 per L) with a marked eosinophilia (78%, 15·3 × 109 per L) and slightly elevated liver enzymes (alanine aminotransferase 101 U/L). An acute appendicitis was suspected and laparoscopic appendectomy was performed.Unexpectedly, intraoperative macroscopic inspection of the liver showed raised white spots on its surface (figure). A biopsy of the liver was done and necrotic granulomas with mainly eosinophils were seen.
A CT scan of the thorax and abdomen after the appendectomy showed nodular pulmonary infiltrates (figure) and hepatomegaly without any specific lesions. The patient was then referred to our hospital, where in a further interview, he said he had recently completed a 2-month trip to Malawi, where he had frequently been in contact with the fresh water in Lake Malawi; the last time was 5 months before the onset of his symptoms.
We diagnosed Schistosoma haematobium using multiplex real-time PCR of the ejaculate and blood. Examination of the ejaculate under light microscope showed vital S haematobium eggs (figure). Re-examination of histopathological samples from the appendix and the liver (figure) showed granulomas with a predominance of eosinophils surrounding S haematobium eggs.
The antiparasitic drug praziquantel was administered at a dose of 40 mg/kg, orally, for 3 days and the patient made a full clinical recovery.
Schistosomiasis affects more than 250 million people worldwide. Global travel and migration have led to an increase in cases presenting in non-endemic regions. The lengthy delay between exposure and the development of non-specific symptoms means that the disease is commonly misdiagnosed at initial presentation. The discovery of macroscopic white spots on the liver and the accidental detection of S haematobium eggs on liver biopsy are uncommon presentations of S haematobium.
When taking a medical history, questions about travel and migration are—as always—of paramount importance.
image_path: ./data/images/lancet_images/White elevated liver lesions detected during appendectomy.jpg
options: Sarcoidosis, Hepatocellular carcinoma, Schistosomiasis, Toxoplasmosis

A 50-year-old woman with a sudden onset of chest pain, diaphoresis, and nausea was admitted to our hospital; additionally, she reported a 1-month history of shortness of breath and chest pain brought on by moderate activity. She had hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and type 2 diabetes of gestational origin; she was prescribed subcutaneous insulin, dulaglutide, empagliflozin, metformin, rosuvastatin and ezetimibe, fenofibrate, ramipril, aspirin, and omeprazole.
On examination she was generally well; she had a blood pressure of 154/72 mm Hg, pulse of 82 beats per min, and oxygen saturation of 96%. Laboratory investigations showed blood glucose concentration of 138 mg/dL (reference range 70·0–105·0), creatinine concentration 0·9 mg/dL (reference range 0·5–1·0), haemoglobin concentration 10·5 g/dL (reference range 12·0–14·0), and ultrasensitive troponin I 417 pg/mL (reference range 0–12).
An electrocardiogram showed ST-segment depression and T-wave inversion in inferolateral leads; a bedside echocardiogram indicated marked hypokinesia in mid-basal segments of the inferior and inferolateral walls. The patient was taken to the catheterisation laboratory for an early invasive strategy. The coronary angiogram (figure 1) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging (figure 2) showed a critical stenosis in the distal right coronary artery due to an occlusive atherosclerotic plaque.We decided to do a percutaneous coronary intervention: after effective pre-dilatation of the lesion (figure 1), we did a coronary angioplasty using a crystalline sirolimus butylated hydroxytoluene drug-coated balloon (DCB; B Braun Melsungen, Melsungen, Germany) in a single 45 sec inflation, resulting in a good final angiographic result (figure 1).
OCT imaging after angioplasty showed hyperechoic particles in the endothelium of the DCB-treated segment (figure 2), in a variety of different patterns (figure 3); notably, the particles caused shadowing effects like those generated by the struts of metallic drug-eluting stents (figure 3).Follow-up coronary angiography 28 days later showed continued patency of the previously stenotic segment—indicative of a favourable angiographic result (figure 1); OCT imaging showed that in some sections of the artery most of the strut-like shadowing and the particles had disappeared (figure 2). In some parts of the artery, however, a few particles remained embedded in the endothelium (figure 2)—suggesting that while most particles had been absorbed, a few continued to be endothelialised and in the process of absorption.
DCBs treat atherosclerotic plaques with antiproliferative agents, similarly to drug-eluting stents but without leaving any permanent metallic stent scaffold—a strategy also known as leave nothing behind. We believe this case shows how sirolimus is deposited and subsequently absorbed within the coronary endothelium after DCB angioplasty (video; appendix).

input: A 56-year-old man undergoing treatment for a prostatic acinar adenocarcinoma was referred to us in May, 2014, for assessment of a massive right pleural effusion (figure). Although the effusion was large, he had only mild shortness of breath and was admitted originally for urinary incontinence. A pleural aspiration showed black pleural fluid (figure). This fluid was determined to be an exudate with very high concentrations of protein (85 g/L; serum protein 56 g/L), lactate dehydrogenase, and amylase. We drained about 3 L of this black pleural fluid from the patient over the following 24 h. Fibreoptic bronchoscopy was normal. However, a thoracoscopy showed nodularity of the visceral and parietal pleura with significant pleural thickening. Pleural fluid cytology showed groups of neoplastic cells arranged in balls, gland, and papillioid configuration in a haemorrhagic background with mesothelial cells and mixed population of inflammatory cells. Immunohistochemistry studies favoured a diagnosis of an adenocarcinoma of pulmonary origin. Percutaneous and thoracoscopic pleural biopsies also confirmed this diagnosis. The patient is receiving treatment for lung and prostate cancer and at last follow-up in February, 2015, he had poor performance status and the pleural effusion was persisting.Black pleural effusions are extremely rare and have been reported previously in patients with pleural infections caused by Aspergillus niger and Rhizopus oryzae, metastatic melanoma, adenocarcinoma of the lung, pancreaticopleural fistula, oesophageal perforation during activated charcoal treatment for a drug overdose, and in patients actively using crack cocaine. The black pleural fluid in our patient was most likely due to haemolysis and the presence of haemosiderin-laden macrophages after a massive bleed into the pleura. The absence of clinically significant symptoms in spite of the massive effusion and the fact that the fluid was black and not red suggest that the fluid collected over a prolonged period of time and that the bleeding would have occurred a long time before presentation. Increased concentrations of amylase in the pleural fluid, as noted in our patient, are commonly seen in patients with lung cancer—most frequently in those with adenocarcinomas.
options: Pleural infection with Aspergillus niger, Adenocarcinoma of the lung, Pancreaticopleural fistula, All of the above

A 78-year-old man with primary central nervous system lymphoma was transferred to our cancer centre for further treatment. The patient had been diagnosed 3 months earlier after he presented to another hospital with back pain, numbness, and tingling in all extremities; he had two cycles of rituximab and high-dose methotrexate, which had produced a partial response. The patient had also been given dexamethasone for cerebral oedema; his medical history included type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and coronary artery disease. He was originally from a country with a high prevalence of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection.
The patient's Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status score ranged from 3 to 4 due to the aggressive cancer; we planned to give him two additional cycles of rituximab and high-dose methotrexate and continue dexamethasone.
2 months after admission—the patient had completed one rituximab combined with methotrexate cycle and started the second—treatment was discontinued due to worsening cognitive function and chemotherapy-related leukoencephalopathy; whole brain radiotherapy was then started. A week later the patient was allowed home to continue treatment as an outpatient.
4 weeks later, the patient was readmitted with nausea, anorexia, increased daytime somnolence, and elevated liver transaminase levels (figure). On examination he was lethargic, but we found no clinical findings—including scleral icterus or ascites—compatible with cirrhosis. Notably, baseline HBV serology tests using an ADVIA Centaur XP immunoassay system (Siemens Diagnostics, Tarrytown, NY, USA) had been done 2 months before chemotherapy was initiated at the previous hospital, with non-reactive hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis B core antibody (HBcAb) total results. He was not tested for hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs). However, on re-testing at our centre using an ARCHITECT analyser (Abbott Laboratories, Abbott Park, IL, USA) we found reactive HBsAg and hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) results but with a persistently non-reactive HBcAb total result; non-reactive anti-HBs; and the HBV-DNA level was 14 100 000 IU/mL, log10 7·15 IU/mL (COBAS HBV assay, Roche Molecular Systems), indicating HBV reactivation with hepatitis flare but without liver failure. FibroTest (Mayo Clinic Laboratories) findings were compatible with F4 fibrosis—but liver ultrasonography with elastography showed normal echogenicity. Tests for total and IgM antibody to hepatitis B core antigen (IgM anti-HBc), HBeAg, hepatitis D total antibody, hepatitis E RNA, herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 DNA, and cytomegalovirus DNA in blood were negative. The HBV genotype was B. No HBV polymerase, precore, or basal core promoter mutations were detected.Entecavir, 0·5 mg orally daily, was started, which produced a good virologic response (figure).
At follow-up 8 months later, the patient was receiving cancer treatment with zanubrutinib plus entecavir and his HBV DNA level was undetectable.
Seronegative occult HBV infection, if reactivated, can cause life-threatening disease in cancer patients; the infection can occur without finding traditional markers—including HBsAg and total anti-HBc, and anti-HBs. The significance and seriousness of the reactivation reinforces the importance of screening patients for HBsAg, HBcAb, and anti-HBs—and the need to be aware that high-level HBV viraemia and significant liver inflammation may occur in the absence of these serum markers, as occurred in our patient.
The prevalence of seronegative occult HBV infection ranges from less than 0·5% among US blood donors to 6% among blood donors from high-HBV-endemicity areas. The wide range may be explained using low-sensitivity assays not standardised or validated and by the lack of a standardised definition of seronegative occult HBV infection. The diagnosis of this condition requires a high degree of epidemiological and clinical suspicion.
options: Chronic HBV infection, False-reactive HBV, Seropositive occult HBV infection, Seronegative occult HBV infection

A 38-year-old woman attended our hospital with a 1-week history of shortness of breath and intermittent chest pain.The patient had Down syndrome and had previously had a ventricular septal defect (VSD) repaired when she was an infant.
On examination, the patient had a blood pressure of 99/77 mm Hg, a heart rate of 98 beats per min, a respiratory rate of 35 breaths per min, and oxygen saturation of 95%. Faint crackles were heard in both lung bases and a 3/6 systolic murmur, heard best at the upper sternal border, radiated to the carotid artery.
A chest x-ray showed a large diaphragmatic hernia, which was confirmed by abdominal CT scan. Laboratory investigations showed a normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 8·0 g/dL; normal 11·5–15 and mean corpuscular volume 96 fL; normal 80–100). The blood urea nitrogen was 8·0 mg/dL (normal 6–24) and troponin concentration was 0·573 ng/mL (normal 0–0·04).
The patient had an uneventful hernia repair and was allowed home 10 days later with plans for an outpatient cardiology appointment to review the murmur. However, 3 days after leaving hospital, she developed acute respiratory failure. A cardiac CT scan, at that stage, showed a bicuspid aortic valve with calcific aortic stenosis (figure). A transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed a heavily calcified aortic valve, but we were unable to say whether it was bicuspid or unicuspid (figure); critical aortic stenosis and moderate-to-severe aortic regurgitation were present. The aortic valve area was 0·8 cm2 with mean gradient of 77 mm Hg. Additionally, the aortic root was mildly dilated, and the calculated ejection fraction was 46%.
The patient was taken to theatre and the aortic valve was replaced with a bioprosthetic valve; multiplanar reconstruction imaging from an intraoperative transoesophageal echocardiogram showed possible unicuspid aortic valve (figure). And indeed, gross pathological examination of the excised valve confirmed a unicuspid aortic valve with multifocal calcification and a single non-fenestrated raphe (figure). Microscopic examination of a sample of the valve showed moderate calcification and fibrosis.
At follow-up 3 months later, the mean systolic gradient across the prosthetic valve was 17 mm Hg, the ejection fraction had improved to 52%, and there was mild prosthetic regurgitation.
Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is commonly associated with congenital heart defects, occurring in 40–50% of patients. The most common heart defects are atrioventricular septal defects (30%), followed by atrial septum defect (25%), VSD (22%), and patent ductus arteriosus (5%), coarctation of the aorta (5%), and tetralogy of Fallot (3%).
While neonates with trisomy 21 are routinely screened for cardiovascular abnormalities, some abnormalities—such as a unicuspid aortic valve in our patient—do not manifest themselves until adolescence or adulthood. Complex aortic valve pathology can cause stenosis and regurgitation in young adults; physical examination and imaging studies are key in identifying newly developed murmurs and patients should be treated promptly. Finally, distinguishing between bicuspid and unicuspid aortic valvular morphology can be difficult: both transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiograms have clear limitations in aiding the clinician to differentiate between them.

input:
A 22-year-old woman with a history of gradually worsening headache, who had developed nausea, vomiting, and diplopia within the past month, was referred to the Department of Neurosurgery of Hospital de Santo António (Porto, Portugal) in June, 2017. Initial neurological examination and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies were unremarkable. Lumbar puncture opening pressure was elevated. The patient had no lesions evoking a congenital phakomatosis or neurocutaneous melanosis, including no nevus of Ota. MRI of the neuroaxis showed mild hydrocephalus and discrete disperse leptomeningeal enhancement of the cranial and spinal nerves (figure, A). Complete physical examination, including observation by ophthalmology and dermatology, followed by whole-body CT scan and scintigraphy, excluded the presence of other lesions. She was proposed for ventricle–peritoneal shunt placement and open brain biopsy. Biopsy analysis showed leptomeningeal thickening, with melanin-containing cells, low mitotic count, and no cellular atypia or brain invasion. Staining was positive for HMB45 and Melan-A, but she tested negative for the BRAFV600E mutation. These findings were consistent with meningeal melanocytosis. Her symptoms improved with shunting.3 months later, she was admitted to the hospital with shunt obstruction, and CSF collected during shunt revision showed cells with nuclear atypia, dark macronucleoli, and positive for melanic pigment, suggestive of melanoma. Off-label treatment with immune checkpoint blockade was considered in combination with radiotherapy, but rapid progression with biplegia and sphincter anomalies, followed by tetraplegia and respiratory depression, ensued. MRI at this stage showed syringobulbia, strong leptomeningeal enhancement of the cranial and spinal nerves, with exuberant filling of the spinal subarachnoid spaces and lumbar cistern (figure, B). She died 4 months after disease presentation.
Primary CNS malignant melanoma is a rare disease. It can be divided into nodular intraparenchymal and diffuse leptomeningeal patterns. The differential diagnosis for a diffusely disseminated leptomeningeal disease includes leptomeningeal carcinomatosis; disseminated primary brain tumours, such as diffuse leptomeningeal glioneuronal tumour; lymphoma; infectious meningitis; and inflammatory conditions, including sarcoidosis. Primary leptomeningeal melanocytosis is an extremely rare and aggressive type of primary CNS melanoma, and few published reports exist. Classically described treatments include radiotherapy and chemotherapy, but recent successes with BRAF inhibitors and immune checkpoint inhibitors in metastatic CNS melanoma suggest the potential of these drugs to treat CNS melanoma.
Clinical awareness of this condition and its aggressive course is fundamental for prompt discussion and expeditious initiation of treatments.
options: Diffuse leptomeningeal glioneuronal tumour, Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis, Meningeal melanocytosis, Neuro-sarcoidosis

input: A 48-year-old man was referred to our institution because of shortness of breath and symptoms related to right ventricular dysfunction. His medical history included tuberculosis as a child. Chest radiography showed a calcific ring located at the heart base. Transthoracic echocardiography showed signs of cardiac tamponade. High resolution CT scan showed the calcific ring at the cardiac base reproducing “el corazón espinado” (the sacred heart wrapped in thorns), with incomplete compression at the level of the inferior vena cava. The patient underwent successful pericardectomy (removal of the pericardium). Despite repeated attempts, the diaphragmatic layer of the calcified pericardium was not removed, because of deep penetration of the calcification inside the myocardium of the inferior right and left ventricles. Histology confirmed the tuberculous cause. Chronic calcific pericarditis is an uncommon form of pericardial inflammation. The cause is idiopathic in most cases; tuberculosis is the second most common cause of this syndrome. Pericardial calcifications occur in nearly half the people affected by chronic pericarditis and are often indicative of infective origin. Early pericardiectomy is strongly encouraged in patients suspected of having tuberculous pericarditis with massive calcification, before signs of cardiac tamponade occur.

input:
In January, 2019, a 37-year-old, White man presented to Saint-Etienne University Hospital (France) with relapsed Hodgkin lymphoma. A PET-CT scan showed hypermetabolic adenomegaly above and below the diaphragm, without visceral or bone involvement. Two cycles of intravenous chemotherapy (gemcitabine 800 mg/m2, vinorelbine 15 mg/m2, and pegylated liposomal doxorubicin 10 mg/m2 on days 1 and 8 every 21 days) resulted in a complete metabolic response in March, 2019. Consolidation consisted of double umbilical cord blood transplantation (dUCBT; total nucleated cells 15·4 × 107 cells per kg and 19·1 × 107 cells per kg for each cord, CD34+ cells 6·5 × 105 cells per kg and 7·9 × 105 cells per kg) after an intravenous conditioning regimen (thiotepa 5·0 mg/kg, busulfan 3·2 mg/kg, fludarabine 40 mg/m2, thymoglobulin 5·0 mg/kg). Prevention of graft-versus-host disease involved intravenous ciclosporin (3 mg/kg per day) and myclophenolate mofetil (3 mg/kg per day) 3 days before dUCBT and 1 month after.2 weeks after dUCBT, he had sudden central scotoma (count fingers) in his left eye, mild neck pain, and headaches. Retinal fundus imaging showed an acute central retinopathy with macular haemorrhage (figure A), explained by severe thrombocytopenia (3 × 109 cells per L, nadir of platelet count). There was no coagulation abnormality except hyperfibrinogenaemia (5 g/L). Macular optical coherence tomography confirmed presumed sub-inner limiting membrane haemorrhage, which is less common than sub-hyaloid haemorrhage. The patient was closely monitored during first-line therapy, which consisted of platelet transfusions repeated twice daily over 6 weeks (total number 84) to reach a minimum of 150 × 109 cells per L. For the initial 2 weeks, his thrombocytopenia was transfusion-refractory and anti-HLA antibodies were not present.
At 3 weeks of follow-up platelets increased to 20 × 109 cells per L, and fibrin aggregates replaced fresh blood (figure B), preventing good visual recovery. At 6 weeks of follow-up platelets reached 180 × 109 cells per L, and the patient recovered perfect vision (20/20) with almost no fibrin clots and a normal macular appearance (figure C).
The prevalence of retinopathy in patients with severe thrombocytopenia is about 30%. Macular haemorrhage can be sub-hyaloid, sub-inner limiting membrane, or a combination of both; optical coherence tomography can help show the precise location (appendix). Whatever the level of the macular haemorrhage associated with severe thrombocytopenia, first-line therapy does not require invasive ophthalmological treatment (eg, intravitreal injection of recombinant tissue plasminogen activator, anti-VEGF, and gas, laser, or surgery with vitrectomy) conventionally used for other aetiologies with similar clinical presentations (particularly Valsalva retinopathy, Terson retinopathy, and retinal vascular diseases); treatment of the underlying cause (platelet transfusion) initially has the best benefit–risk ratio, considering the fragile background of these patients. Invasive local options should be discussed as second-line therapy, when macular haemorrhage persists despite resolution of severe thrombocytopenia.

input:
A 3-year-old girl was referred to the dermatology department with blonde, straw-like, and unruly hair. The child's parents reported that since birth her hair had been sparse and slow growing. And from about one year of age, her parents had difficulty combing her hair.On clinical examination of the patient's scalp hair, we found the patient had blonde, dry, and glistening hair (figure); her eyebrows and eyelashes were unaffected.
Examination of the hair using light microscopy showed irregular triangle-shaped hair shafts and atypical canals along the hair shaft axis.
Molecular genetic analysis showed the homozygous pathogenic variant c.881C>T (p.Ala294Val) in exon 8 of the PADI3 gene.
Considering together the findings from clinical examination, light microscopy, and genetic analysis, we made a diagnosis of uncombable hair syndrome: a rare hair shaft anomaly that presents in early childhood with blond, glistening, and frizzy hair.
Patients’ scalp hair grows in thick bundles that project out in different directions which makes combing impossible. Additionally, in some cases the rate of hair growth may be slow. Under light microscopy, the hair shafts may appear unaffected, and scanning electron microscopy may be necessary to confirm the presence of triangulated hair shafts and longitudinal grooves along the hair shaft axis. No definitive treatment is yet available, but oral biotin supplementation has been reported to make clinical improvement in some cases. The prognosis is promising as hair texture improves during puberty. In some cases, the condition is associated with brachydactyly, ectodermal dysplasia, juvenile cataract, and oligodontia.
Most cases of uncombable hair syndrome—a condition depicted in the 1845 German children's book Der Struwwelpeter, which translates as “Shock-headed Peter”—are sporadic and autosomal recessive; the responsible pathogenic variants are in the PADI3, TCHH, and TGM3 genes, which encode for proteins involved in hair shaft formation. Employment of molecular genetics in diagnosing this syndrome must now be considered the gold standard. Generally, when diagnosing hair and skin disorders, molecular genetics has the advantage of confirming the clinical diagnosis with greater certainty; risks of family members may also be identified. Additionally, molecular genetic analysis usually only requires saliva or an EDTA blood sample, thus avoiding the employment of more invasive investigations.
options: Hereditary hypotrichosis simplex of the scalp, Menkes kinky hair syndrome, Woolly hair, Uncombable hair syndrome

A 74-year-old female patient presented in November, 2017, with a 3-month history of pain in the upper left thigh. X-ray revealed three osteolytic lesions of the left femur, one of which was breaking the cortical bone. No organomegaly was noted on physical examination. Blood counts and biochemical tests were normal except for mild hypergammaglobulinemia (16·9%) with positive immunofixation for monoclonal immunoglobulin A (0·2 g/dL in the serum, but urine negative).Multiple myeloma was suspected, and whole-body PET scan documented increased fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in several bone sites (SUVmax 4·9–10·9): at the head of humeri, sacrum, iliac wings, right acetabulum, and proximal femurs (figure, A), with extension into the soft tissues surrounding the broken cortex of the left femur.
A routine marrow biopsy from the iliac crest was unexpectedly normal on immunohistology for the plasma cell marker CD138 and the B-cell marker CD20. However, a core biopsy of the left femural neck documented a massive infiltration by mature lymphoid cells with ample cytoplasm and hairy projections positive for CD20, annexin-1 (figure, B), and BRAFV600E, thereby establishing a diagnosis of hairy cell leukaemia.
Morphological and flow-cytometric analyses of peripheral blood did not show any hairy cells, and a sensitive allele-specific PCR assay for BRAFV600E was also negative in both the blood and iliac marrow aspirate.
The patient received chemotherapy with cladribine (0·14 mg/kg per day for 5 consecutive days subcutaneously) and her pain gradually subsided. A PET scan 8 weeks later showed substantially decreased uptake of fluorodeoxyglucose at multiple bone lesions.
Although skeletal involvement can occur in hairy cell leukaemia (in around 3% of cases), patients with hairy cell leukaemia, who are mostly males, usually also present with cytopenias, splenomegaly, circulating hairy cells, and diffuse leukaemic infiltration of the bone marrow. Focal bone lesions accompanied by none of these characteristic features, but rather by a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance as occurred in this woman, represent a challenging differential diagnosis with more frequent neoplasms, especially multiple myeloma.
output: Are frequent in multiple myeloma and rare in hairy cell leukaemia

A 17-year-old transgender man attended our hospital with a 2-month history of intermittent right-sided abdominal pain, nausea, early satiety, profuse night sweats, and 14 kg weight loss.For the past 14 months, he had been undergoing hormonal gender reassignment—female to male—with weekly intramuscular injections of 32 mg of testosterone cypionate.
On examination he showed secondary male sexual characteristics: he had a deep voice and he had facial hair and acne. He was thin with a body-mass index of 18·5 kg/m2. On deep palpation he had increased mild tenderness of the right upper abdominal quadrant, compared to the left side.
MRI of the patient's abdomen showed a 17·5 cm × 7·2 cm × 8·0 cm enhancing mass in the left hemiliver with numerous small surrounding satellite lesions and tumour thrombi in the main, right, and left portal veins (figure). Core needle biopsy of the liver mass showed hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with clear cell change (figure); androgen receptor (AR) nuclear staining was seen in 40% of the cells (figure). Liver tissue outside the tumour was normal—confirmed on staining with trichrome, reticulin, periodic acid-Schiff, and iron.
The patient's serum alpha-fetoprotein concentration was 4320 ng/mL (normal less than 8·3) with a non-reactive hepatitis serology panel—including hepatitis A virus IgM, HBsAg, HBcAg IgM, and hepatitis C virus antibody.
We treated him initially with yttrium-90 (90Y)-loaded glass microspheres (TheraSphere, Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA, USA) at a dose of 160 Gray (Gy), delivered by intra-arterial injection to the involved segments of his liver, 1·48 gigabecquerel (GBq) to segment 4 and 1·87 GBq to segments 2 and 3.
MRI of the patient's abdomen 2 months after the treatment showed new lesions in the right hemiliver (figure) and his alpha-fetoprotein concentration had increased to 10 933 ng/mL. The patient stopped taking the exogenous testosterone after we discussed with him the possible effects it might be having upon the tumour. He was then started on intramuscular injections of leuprolide—a synthetic gonadotropin-releasing hormone—at a dose of 30 mg every 30 days to prevent the development of secondary female sexual characteristics.
He returned for a second treatment of 90Y-loaded glass microspheres to the right hemiliver at a dose of 151 Gy: 4·42 GBq to segments 5–8. He was found to have partial radiographic response in both the right and left hemiliver lesions and subsequently received additional 90Y-loaded glass microsphere treatment. The patient continues to be monitored for progression of the disease. Future treatment—if necessary—may include systemic targeted therapy or immunotherapy in a clinical trial.
HCC is mostly found in men and studies have linked the AR to development of the disease. AR expression and its role in HCC remains unclear. AR is overexpressed in the nuclei of approximately 74% of HCCs in men and 38% in women; it is associated with advanced disease and poor survival. Preclinical work suggests AR may play a role in the early development of HCC, but knocking out AR signalling in the later stages of the disease does not attenuate tumour growth. AR staining is not routinely obtained in patients with HCC and antiandrogen therapy is not indicated.
The relationship between exogenous testosterone and development and progression of HCC in peripubertal transgender patients is unknown. Further, it is unknown whether continuation of testosterone in patients positive for AR nuclear staining affects the outcome of the disease (video).
options: Male sex, Liver cirrhosis, Acute hepatitis A infection, Haemochromatosis
